name: list-criteria

density.note: one criterion with a short proof, not a spec

description: Numbered criteria list — each requirement is a row with rationale.
purpose: Use to enumerate the criteria a decision must meet, in priority order. Numbering signals weight; each row reads as a complete requirement.

criteria.description: One li per criterion. The lead text is the criterion title — it renders bold automatically (no `**…**` needed); follow it with a nested `- rationale` bullet.

skeleton:
<!-- _class: list-criteria -->

## What every decision must satisfy.

1. First criterion
   - Short rationale for why this matters.
2. Second criterion
   - Short rationale.
3. Third criterion
   - Short rationale.
4. Fourth criterion
   - Short rationale.
sample:
<!-- _class: list-criteria -->

## Criteria are gates: clear them in order.

1. State the bar
   - Each criterion is a pass-or-fail line, not a preference.
2. Order by veto power
   - The criterion most likely to kill goes first.
3. Keep the list short
   - Three gates decide; six gates stall.

stressDoc.sample:
<!-- _class: list-criteria -->

## Five gates is the most one decision should clear.

1. The first gate
   - A criterion at the hard budget states the bar and the evidence that clears it, in one breath.
2. The second gate
   - Twenty-two words is the ceiling; this clause is written to sit just under it, deliberately.
3. The third gate
   - Middle gates read fastest — put the contested one here.
4. The fourth gate
   - Attention thins; shorten the clauses as the list descends.
5. The fifth gate
   - The stop. A sixth gate means the bar is a rubric, not a decision.

whenToUse.title: Criteria that must all be satisfied
whenToUse.body: When the audience needs to read each requirement as a complete gate, not a suggestion. The numbered ledger format signals 'these are the rules' rather than 'here are some options'.

whenToUse.title: Order encodes priority
whenToUse.body: The leading-zero counter (`01`, `02`, …) reads as rank. Put the load-bearing criterion first; the audience uses position as a weight.

whenToUse.title: Three to six rows
whenToUse.body: Below three the ledger feels under-furnished; above six the row gap closes and the audience loses scannability. Group adjacent criteria or split into two slides.

antiPatterns.title: Parallel options, not gates
antiPatterns.body: If the items are alternatives the audience is choosing between, use `cards-grid` or `verdict-grid`. list-criteria is for requirements all of which must hold.

antiPatterns.title: Rationale longer than two lines
antiPatterns.body: Each row is a one-sentence rationale. If a criterion needs a paragraph, lift it to `list-steps` or `split-panel` where the body has room to breathe.

antiPatterns.title: Missing criterion title
antiPatterns.body: The lead line on each li — rendered bold automatically — is what makes the ledger scannable. A naked sentence per row reads as paragraph soup; the title is the structure.

related.name: list-steps
related.when: rows are procedural steps with longer body, not gating criteria

related.name: list-tabular
related.when: rows carry structured metadata alongside the name and description

commonMistakes.mistake: Manually bolding the criterion title with `**…**`.
commonMistakes.fix: The lead text of each `li` is auto-lifted to `<strong>` by the engine's slot-label-lift step, which already skips a lead that's already bolded — a manually bolded lead and a plain one produce byte-identical output. Wrapping it yourself is a harmless no-op, not a defect, but it's also unnecessary — write plain text and let the lift handle the weight.

commonMistakes.mistake: Nesting the rationale as a numbered sub-list (`1.`) instead of a bullet (`-`).
commonMistakes.fix: The rationale styling only targets a nested `ul` — a numbered sub-list (`1.`) falls back to default list markup instead of the muted, unmarked rationale line.
